title: Not by Friction Alone
author: Lily M. Abadal
source: Wisdom in the Machine Age (wisdominthemachineage.substack.com), September 25, 2026
summary: Philosopher and educator Lily Abadal examines the popular claim that adding friction is the answer to AI in education. She separates two versions: the Socratic AI solution, where tools like SchoolAI and Khan Academy are designed not to give answers, and the Socratic Student solution, where students are taught to ask the bot to critique their reasoning. She argues the first fails because students who do not want to be questioned will simply use another tool, and the second presumes virtues students have not yet developed. A deeper objection is moral formation: conversations with chatbots avoid the inconvenience of people, but those inconveniences are exactly where patience, humility, resilience, and civility are learned. Her conclusion is that friction cannot be taught through unbounded access to AI. Instead, instructors should structure frequent small-group dialogue, debate, and listening exercises with real people.
points: Friction-by-design chatbots and friction-by-student prompting are both inadequate, because students can route around the first and lack the virtues required for the second.
Requiring students to submit chats with an assigned friction bot is easy to evade by running a second, answer-giving bot in another tab.
Dialogue with humans is morally formative in a way chatbot dialogue is not, since it builds patience, humility, resilience, and civility.
Students should not be expected to supply formative friction themselves inside a limitless tool that does not require it by design.
Teachers should prioritise structured, frequent peer dialogue, small-group practice, and live debate over AI-mediated conversation.
quotes: In the spirit of friction—and Socrates—I’d like to push back on both of these as panaceas to the AI problem in education. Neither of these solves the risks that integrating AI in education has posed.
The Socratic solution would be great if all students wanted to talk to Socrates. I wish that were the case.
Dialogue is morally formative insofar as it helps us understand how to better live in community with others—that is, other human beings.

Because humans are all these things, we need particular virtues to live well in community together—like patience and humility and resilience and civility. These are the kinds of virtues learned by lots of practice having hard discussions with living, breathing people.
That is, students should not be assumed to have the virtues Socrates possessed that allowed him to ask the kinds of questions he asked.
Students should not be expected to bring the formative friction themselves. This is especially the case when they are expected to bring it to a limitless sandbox that does not require it by design.
The best and most sure-fire way to teach students to dialogue well is to structure Socratic dialogue in class with other people—and to do it often, and with the structure necessary to improve.
